claim: The slx9-1 allele (slx9L108P) causes slow growth at temperatures between 20°C and 30°C, indistinguishable from slx9∆ cells.
source: One allele, slx9L108P, hereafter termed slx9-1, caused slow growth at temperatures between 20°C and 30°C, indistinguishable from slx9∆ cells (Figure 1A, top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental growth assay data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: slx9∆ and slx9-1 cells are not impaired in growth at 37°C.
source: Like slx9∆, slx9-1 cells were not impaired in growth at 37°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental growth assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Slx9 and Slx9-1 are present at similar levels in whole cell lysates.
source: Western analysis of whole cell lysates revealed that Slx9 and Slx9-1 were present at similar levels (Figure 1A, bottom panel), indicating that impaired growth of the slx9-1 strain is not due to reduced levels of the mutant protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A bottom panel.

claim: Impaired growth of the slx9-1 strain is not due to reduced levels of the mutant protein.
source: Western analysis of whole cell lysates revealed that Slx9 and Slx9-1 were present at similar levels (Figure 1A, bottom panel), indicating that impaired growth of the slx9-1 strain is not due to reduced levels of the mutant protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slx9 and Slx9-1 protein levels are similar.

claim: Slx9-GFP localizes primarily to the nucleolus and nucleoplasm.
source: As previously observed, Slx9-GFP localized primarily to the nucleolus, where it co-localized with the nucleolar marker Gar1-mCherry, as well as to the nucleoplasm (Faza et al., 2012 and Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and cited previous work.

claim: Slx9-1-GFP displays an identical localization to Slx9-GFP.
source: Slx9-1-GFP displayed an identical localization (Figure 1B), indicating that the mutant protein is correctly targeted to the nucleolus and nucleoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Slx9-1 mutant protein is correctly targeted to the nucleolus and nucleoplasm.
source: Slx9-1-GFP displayed an identical localization (Figure 1B), indicating that the mutant protein is correctly targeted to the nucleolus and nucleoplasm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slx9-1-GFP shows the same localization as wild-type Slx9-GFP.

claim: Slx9 maximally co-enriches with Enp1-TAP that purifies both the 90S and 40S pre-ribosomes.
source: Slx9 maximally co-enriched with Enp1-TAP that purifies both the 90S and 40S pre-ribosomes (Faza et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Enp1-TAP from slx9-1 cells co-enriches at least as much Slx9-1 mutant protein as Slx9.
source: A similar purification from slx9-1 cells revealed that Enp1-TAP co-enriched at least as much Slx9-1 mutant protein as Slx9 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tandem affinity purification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Slx9-1 is correctly expressed, localized, and recruited to 40S pre-ribosomes.
source: Together, these data show that Slx9-1 is correctly expressed, localized, and recruited to 40S pre-ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations including protein levels, localization, and co-purification data.

claim: slx9∆ cells accumulate the small subunit reporter uS5-GFP in the nucleoplasm.
source: Previous studies showed that slx9∆ cells accumulate the small subunit reporter uS5-GFP (yeast Rps2, nomenclature according to Ban et al., 2014) and 20S pre-rRNA in the nucleoplasm (Li et al., 2009; Faza et al., 2012), indicating a defect in 40S pre-ribosome export.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: slx9∆ cells accumulate 20S pre-rRNA in the nucleoplasm.
source: Previous studies showed that slx9∆ cells accumulate the small subunit reporter uS5-GFP (yeast Rps2, nomenclature according to Ban et al., 2014) and 20S pre-rRNA in the nucleoplasm (Li et al., 2009; Faza et al., 2012), indicating a defect in 40S pre-ribosome export.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: slx9∆ cells have a defect in 40S pre-ribosome export.
source: Previous studies showed that slx9∆ cells accumulate the small subunit reporter uS5-GFP (yeast Rps2, nomenclature according to Ban et al., 2014) and 20S pre-rRNA in the nucleoplasm (Li et al., 2009; Faza et al., 2012), indicating a defect in 40S pre-ribosome export.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of nucleoplasmic accumulation of export reporters and supported by citations.

claim: slx9-1 cells show a strong nuclear accumulation of uS5-GFP, similar to that observed in slx9∆ cells.
source: Whereas WT cells displayed cytoplasmic uS5-GFP localization, slx9-1 cells showed a strong nuclear accumulation of this reporter, similar to that observed in slx9∆ cells (Faza et al., 2012 and Figure 1D, top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and cited previous work.

claim: WT cells display cytoplasmic uS5-GFP localization.
source: Whereas WT cells displayed cytoplasmic uS5-GFP localization, slx9-1 cells showed a strong nuclear accumulation of this reporter, similar to that observed in slx9∆ cells (Faza et al., 2012 and Figure 1D, top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FISH of 20S pre-rRNA in WT cells shows a strong nucleolar Cy3-ITS1 signal with virtually no nucleoplasmic staining.
source: As expected, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) of 20S pre-rRNA in WT cells showed a strong nucleolar Cy3-ITS1 signal (red) with virtually no nucleoplasmic staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH experimental data described in the text.

claim: slx9-1 cells display a nucleoplasmic signal of Cy3-ITS1 localization, which co-localizes with the DAPI signal.
source: In contrast, slx9-1 cells displayed a nucleoplasmic signal of Cy3-ITS1 localization, which co-localized with the DAPI signal (Figure 1D, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1D bottom panel.

claim: slx9-1 cells are impaired in 40S pre-ribosome export.
source: These data indicate that slx9-1 cells, like slx9∆ cells (Faza et al., 2012), are impaired in 40S pre-ribosome export.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the nucleoplasmic accumulation of uS5-GFP and 20S pre-rRNA in slx9-1 cells.

claim: Slx9-1 is recruited to the 40S pre-ribosome but fails to fulfill its function in nuclear export of the pre-ribosomal cargo.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Slx9-1 is recruited to the 40S pre-ribosome but fails to fulfill its function in nuclear export of the pre-ribosomal cargo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that Slx9-1 is recruited to pre-ribosomes but cells show export defects.

claim: Mutations in MEX67 and MTR2 (mex67Δloop and mtr2Δloop116-137) are synthetically lethal when combined with the slx9Δ mutant.
source: Mutations in MEX67 and MTR2 (mex67Δloop and mtr2Δloop116-137), which encode the essential transport receptor Mex67-Mtr2, are synthetically lethal when combined with the slx9Δ mutant (Faza et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: slx9∆ displays a synthetic growth defect with a strain expressing Rrp12-GFP.
source: In addition, we found that slx9∆ displayed a synthetic growth defect with a strain expressing Rrp12-GFP (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Rrp12 is a 40S pre-ribosome export factor that directly interacts with FG-rich nucleoporins.
source: Rrp12 is a 40S pre-ribosome export factor that directly interacts with FG-rich nucleoporins (Oeffinger et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Slx9 shuttles between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
source: As controls, we used the shuttling 40S assembly factor Enp1 and the non-shuttling nucleolar protein Gar1 fused to GFP. Whereas Gar1-GFP was never seen in the nucleus of kar1-1 cells (red signal), both Enp1-GFP and Slx9-GFP localized to both nuclei (Figure 2B). These data are consistent with the shuttling of Slx9 between the nuclear and the cytoplasmic compartments.
evidence: The claim is supported by heterokaryon assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Enp1 is a shuttling 40S assembly factor.
source: As controls, we used the shuttling 40S assembly factor Enp1 and the non-shuttling nucleolar protein Gar1 fused to GFP.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge used as a control.

claim: Gar1 is a non-shuttling nucleolar protein.
source: As controls, we used the shuttling 40S assembly factor Enp1 and the non-shuttling nucleolar protein Gar1 fused to GFP.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge used as a control.

claim: Gar1-GFP was never seen in the nucleus of kar1-1 cells in heterokaryon assays.
source: Whereas Gar1-GFP was never seen in the nucleus of kar1-1 cells (red signal), both Enp1-GFP and Slx9-GFP localized to both nuclei (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by heterokaryon assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both Enp1-GFP and Slx9-GFP localized to both nuclei in heterokaryon assays.
source: Whereas Gar1-GFP was never seen in the nucleus of kar1-1 cells (red signal), both Enp1-GFP and Slx9-GFP localized to both nuclei (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by heterokaryon assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Slx9 does not form a trimeric export complex with Crm1 and RanQLGTP.
source: Unlike Ssb1C (Maurer et al., 2001 and Figure 2C, lane 8), Slx9 was unable to form a trimeric export complex with Crm1 and RanQLGTP (Figure 2C, lane 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C and cited previous work.

claim: Ssb1C forms a trimeric export complex with Crm1 and RanQLGTP.
source: Unlike Ssb1C (Maurer et al., 2001 and Figure 2C, lane 8), Slx9 was unable to form a trimeric export complex with Crm1 and RanQLGTP (Figure 2C, lane 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C and cited previous work.

claim: Slx9 directly binds RanQLGTP.
source: Surprisingly, these studies revealed that Slx9 directly bound RanQLGTP (Figure 2C, lane 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Slx9 does not contain a functional NES.
source: Therefore, although Slx9 does not contain a functional NES, it is a Ran-binding protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slx9 does not form a trimeric complex with Crm1 and RanGTP.

claim: Slx9 is a Ran-binding protein.
source: Therefore, although Slx9 does not contain a functional NES, it is a Ran-binding protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that Slx9 directly binds RanQLGTP.

claim: Slx9 interacts exclusively with RanGTP and not RanGDP.
source: We found that, like Yrb1, Slx9 interacted exclusively with RanGTP (Figure 2D, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Yrb1 interacts exclusively with RanGTP.
source: We found that, like Yrb1, Slx9 interacted exclusively with RanGTP (Figure 2D, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ntf2 binds to RanGDP.
source: As controls, we used Ntf2, the import factor for RanGDP (Ribbeck et al., 1998; Smith et al., 1998 and Figure 2D, lane 8) and the yeast RanBP1 homolog Yrb1 that binds to RanGTP (Schlenstedt et al., 1995 and Figure 2D, lane 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2D and cited previous work.

claim: Slx9 is a shuttling RanGTP-binding protein.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that Slx9 is a shuttling RanGTP-binding protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that Slx9 shuttles and binds specifically to RanGTP.

claim: slx9-1 cells genetically interact with mex67 and mtr2 mutants (mex67∆loop and mtr2∆116-137).
source: Furthermore, like slx9∆ cells, slx9-1 cells genetically interacted with mex67 and mtr2 mutants (mex67∆loop and mtr2∆116-137) and rrp12-GFP (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: slx9-1 cells genetically interact with rrp12-GFP.
source: Furthermore, like slx9∆ cells, slx9-1 cells genetically interacted with mex67 and mtr2 mutants (mex67∆loop and mtr2∆116-137) and rrp12-GFP (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a decrease of approximately 50% in the levels of RanQLGTP bound to Slx9-1 as compared to Slx9.
source: We found a decrease of approximately 50% in the levels of RanQLGTP bound to Slx9-1 as compared to Slx9 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Slx9-1 is modestly impaired in binding RanQLGTP.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that Slx9-1 is modestly impaired in binding RanQLGTP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of approximately 50% reduction in RanQLGTP binding to Slx9-1.

claim: A conserved basic patch on Ran is involved in the interaction with known Ran-binding proteins.
source: A conserved basic patch on Ran is involved in the interaction with known Ran-binding proteins (Nilsson et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RanQLGTP mutants (RanQLGTPRKAA and RanQLGTPRKEE) bind weakly to the importin β-like transport receptor Kap123.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Nilsson et al., 2001), these RanQLGTP mutants bound weakly to the importin β-like transport receptor, Kap123 (Figure 3A, compare lane 10 with lanes 11 and 12), and interacted more strongly with the RanBP1 homolog Yrb1 (Figure 3A, compare lane 6 with lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3A and cited previous work.

claim: RanQLGTP mutants (RanQLGTPRKAA and RanQLGTPRKEE) interact more strongly with the RanBP1 homolog Yrb1 compared to wild-type RanQLGTP.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Nilsson et al., 2001), these RanQLGTP mutants bound weakly to the importin β-like transport receptor, Kap123 (Figure 3A, compare lane 10 with lanes 11 and 12), and interacted more strongly with the RanBP1 homolog Yrb1 (Figure 3A, compare lane 6 with lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3A and cited previous work.

claim: The interactions between Slx9 and RanQLGTP mutants (RanQLGTPRKAA and RanQLGTPRKEE) are impaired, with the charge reversal mutant having a more severe effect than the alanine mutant.
source: Pull down studies of Slx9 and these Ran mutants showed that the interactions between Slx9 and these two Ran mutants were impaired, with the charge reversal mutant having a more severe effect than the alanine mutant (Figure 3A, compare lane 2 with lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The basic patch of RanQLGTP contributes to Slx9 binding.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that, similar to Kap123, Slx9 binding to RanQLGTP involves the basic patch.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutations in the basic patch impair Slx9 binding to RanQLGTP.

claim: The C-terminal acidic tail of Ran (-DEDDAL) plays a crucial role in the interaction with small RanGTP-binding proteins such as Yrb1.
source: The C-terminal acidic tail of Ran (-DEDDAL) plays a crucial role in the interaction with small RanGTP-binding proteins such as Yrb1.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: RanQLGTP lacking the C-terminal acidic tail (Ran∆CQLGTP) fails to interact with Yrb1 in vitro.
source: As expected, RanQLGTP lacking the C-terminal acidic tail (Ran∆CQL GTP) failed to interact with Yrb1 in vitro (Maurer et al., 2001 and Figure 3B, lane 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3B and cited previous work.

claim: Ran∆CQLGTP binds stronger to Slx9 compared to RanQLGTP.
source: In contrast to Yrb1, Ran∆CQLGTP bound stronger to Slx9 compared to RanQLGTP (Figure 3B, compare lane 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The enhanced interaction between Ran∆CQLGTP and Slx9 is specific.
source: This enhanced interaction was specific, since Kap123 bound Ran∆CQLGTP and RanQLGTP to a similar extent (Figure 3B, compare lanes 8 and 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3B showing that Kap123 does not show differential binding.

claim: The C-terminal acidic tail of Ran negatively regulates RanGTP:Slx9 interactions.
source: These data suggest that the C-terminal acidic tail of Ran negatively regulates RanGTP:Slx9 interactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that removal of the acidic tail enhances Slx9 binding.

claim: Cells lacking the RanGTP- and Crm1-binding protein Yrb2 (yrb2Δ) exhibit strong nucleoplasmic accumulation of uS5-GFP and 20S pre-rRNA.
source: Cells lacking the RanGTP- and Crm1-binding protein Yrb2 (yrb2Δ) exhibit strong nucleoplasmic accumulation of uS5-GFP and 20S pre-rRNA as well as reduced abundance of 40S subunits (Moy and Silver, 2002; Altvater et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: yrb2Δ cells have reduced abundance of 40S subunits.
source: Cells lacking the RanGTP- and Crm1-binding protein Yrb2 (yrb2Δ) exhibit strong nucleoplasmic accumulation of uS5-GFP and 20S pre-rRNA as well as reduced abundance of 40S subunits (Moy and Silver, 2002; Altvater et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: mex67Δloop and mtr2Δloop116-137 are synthetically lethal with yrb2Δ.
source: In addition, mex67Δloop and mtr2Δloop116-137 are synthetically lethal with yrb2Δ (Faza et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Both slx9∆ and slx9-1 are synthetically lethal with yrb2∆.
source: Both slx9∆ and slx9-1 were synthetically lethal with yrb2∆ (Figure 2A), suggesting that Slx9 and Yrb2 functionally overlap to ensure proper nuclear export of 40S pre-ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Slx9 and Yrb2 functionally overlap to ensure proper nuclear export of 40S pre-ribosomes.
source: Both slx9∆ and slx9-1 were synthetically lethal with yrb2∆ (Figure 2A), suggesting that Slx9 and Yrb2 functionally overlap to ensure proper nuclear export of 40S pre-ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the synthetic lethality between slx9 mutants and yrb2∆.

claim: Yrb2 and its human homolog, RanBP3, stimulate the assembly of Crm1-export complexes on certain NES-containing cargos by cooperatively binding Crm1 and RanGTP.
source: Yrb2 and its human homolog, RanBP3, stimulate the assembly of Crm1-export complexes on certain NES-containing cargos by cooperatively binding Crm1 and RanGTP (Englmeier et al., 2001; Lindsay et al., 2001; Koyama et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Slx9 binds RanGTP, but not Crm1.
source: However, our interaction studies showed that Slx9 binds RanGTP, but not Crm1 (Figure 2C, lane 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: hLtv1 and hRio2 have been shown to bind Crm1 in the presence of RanGTP.
source: Two 40S pre-ribosome-associated factors, hLtv1 and hRio2, have been shown to bind Crm1 in the presence of RanGTP (Zemp et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Yeast Ltv1 and yeast Rio2 form trimeric complexes with Crm1 and RanQLGTP via a cooperative mechanism in vitro.
source: In agreement with these studies, we found that yeast Ltv1 and yeast Rio2 formed trimeric complexes with Crm1 and RanQLGTP via a cooperative mechanism in vitro (Figure 4A, lanes 4 and 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The C-terminal regions of Rio2 and Ltv1 are predicted to contain a NES.
source: Moreover, the C-terminal regions of these proteins are predicted to contain a NES (Zemp et al., 2009; Merwin et al., 2014 and Figure 4A, top panel), and indeed, Rio2 and Ltv1 mutant proteins lacking NESs were unable to form trimeric export complexes (Figure 4A, lanes 8 and 16).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and predictions.

claim: Rio2 and Ltv1 mutant proteins lacking NESs are unable to form trimeric export complexes.
source: Moreover, the C-terminal regions of these proteins are predicted to contain a NES (Zemp et al., 2009; Merwin et al., 2014 and Figure 4A, top panel), and indeed, Rio2 and Ltv1 mutant proteins lacking NESs were unable to form trimeric export complexes (Figure 4A, lanes 8 and 16).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Rio2, but not Ltv1, interacts weakly with RanQLGTP, independent of Crm1.
source: Western analyses revealed that Rio2, but not Ltv1, interacted weakly with RanQLGTP, independent of Crm1 (Figure 4A, lane 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ltv1 and Rio2 co-enrich with the Enp1-TAP particle that also maximally co-purifies Slx9.
source: Ltv1 and Rio2 co-enrich with the Enp1-TAP particle that also maximally co-purifies Slx9 (Figure 1C; Schütz et al., 2014) suggesting that these NES-containing proteins might interact with Slx9.
evidence: The claim is supported by purification data shown in Figure 1C and cited previous work.

claim: Slx9 directly binds to Rio2 but not to Ltv1.
source: Slx9 directly bound to Rio2 but not to Ltv1 (Figure 4B, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GST-Slx9 interacts with Rio2 but not with the essential 60S pre-ribosome-associated NES-containing adaptor Nmd3.
source: Conversely, GST-Slx9 interacted with Rio2 but not with the essential 60S pre-ribosome-associated NES-containing adaptor Nmd3 (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The GST-Rio2:Slx9 complex efficiently recruits RanQLGTP.
source: Moreover, the GST-Rio2:Slx9 complex efficiently recruited RanQLGTP (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The level of RanQLGTP recruitment to GST-Rio2 is not affected by the prior presence or absence of Slx9.
source: The level of recruitment was not affected by the prior presence or absence of Slx9, since GST-Rio2 saturated with Slx9 recruited similar amounts of RanQLGTP (Figure 5B, compare top and bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The levels of RanQLGTP recruitment to GST-Slx9 are not affected by the presence or absence of Rio2.
source: Also, the levels of RanQLGTP recruitment to GST-Slx9 were not affected by the presence or absence of Rio2 (Figure 5C, compare top and bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Rio2 binds Slx9 and RanQLGTP using distinct surfaces.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that Rio2 binds Slx9 and RanQLGTP using distinct surfaces.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slx9 and RanQLGTP do not compete for binding to Rio2.

claim: The GST-Rio2:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex efficiently recruits Crm1.
source: Only the GST-Rio2:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex efficiently recruited Crm1 (Figure 6B, compare lanes 4 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The GST-Rio2:RanQLGTP complex does not efficiently recruit Crm1.
source: Only the GST-Rio2:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex efficiently recruited Crm1 (Figure 6B, compare lanes 4 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Crm1-recruitment to a GST-Rio2:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex is dependent on the NES of Rio2.
source: The Crm1-recruitment to a GST-Rio2:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex was dependent on the NES of Rio2, since a GST-Rio2∆NES:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex was unable to bind Crm1 (Figure 6B, compare lanes 8 and 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A GST-Rio2∆NES:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex is unable to bind Crm1.
source: The Crm1-recruitment to a GST-Rio2:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex was dependent on the NES of Rio2, since a GST-Rio2∆NES:Slx9:RanQLGTP complex was unable to bind Crm1 (Figure 6B, compare lanes 8 and 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Crm1 recruitment is dependent on the RanQLGTP bound to Rio2.
source: Moreover, Crm1 recruitment was also dependent on the RanQLGTP bound to Rio2, since a GST-Rio2:Slx9 complex was unable to bind Crm1 (Figure 6C, lane 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A GST-Rio2:Slx9 complex is unable to bind Crm1.
source: Moreover, Crm1 recruitment was also dependent on the RanQLGTP bound to Rio2, since a GST-Rio2:Slx9 complex was unable to bind Crm1 (Figure 6C, lane 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In order to recruit Crm1 in a non-cooperative manner, Rio2 must bind to both Slx9 and RanGTP.
source: These studies indicate that, in order to recruit Crm1 in a non-cooperative manner, Rio2 must bind to both Slx9 and RanGTP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that both Slx9 and RanGTP are required for Crm1 recruitment to Rio2.

claim: Rio2 binds Slx9-1.
source: In vitro binding studies revealed that Rio2 binds Slx9-1 (Figure 6D, lane 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Slx9-1 binds at least as well to Rio2 as Slx9.
source: In comparison to the Slx9, Slx9-1 bound at least as well to Rio2 (Figure 6D, compare lane 2 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The GST-Rio2:Slx9-1 complex is able to recruit RanQLGTP.
source: Further, the GST-Rio2:Slx9-1 complex was also able to recruit RanQLGTP (Figure 6D, lane 7), indicating that Slx9-1 is still able to assemble a GST-Rio2:Slx9-1:RanQLGTP complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Slx9-1 is able to assemble a GST-Rio2:Slx9-1:RanQLGTP complex.
source: Further, the GST-Rio2:Slx9-1 complex was also able to recruit RanQLGTP (Figure 6D, lane 7), indicating that Slx9-1 is still able to assemble a GST-Rio2:Slx9-1:RanQLGTP complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the GST-Rio2:Slx9-1 complex recruits RanQLGTP.

claim: The GST-Rio2:Slx9-1:RanQLGTP complex is impaired in loading Crm1.
source: However, this complex was impaired in loading Crm1 (Figure 6D, compare lane 5 and 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Slx9 promotes assembly of a Crm1-export complex on Rio2.
source: Therefore, we suggest that Slx9 promotes assembly of a Crm1-export complex on Rio2, and that this function relies on a proper interaction between Slx9 and RanGTP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that Slx9 is required for efficient Crm1 recruitment to Rio2 and that Slx9-1 with impaired RanGTP binding is defective in this function.

claim: Slx9's function in promoting Crm1-export complex assembly relies on a proper interaction between Slx9 and RanGTP.
source: Therefore, we suggest that Slx9 promotes assembly of a Crm1-export complex on Rio2, and that this function relies on a proper interaction between Slx9 and RanGTP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slx9-1 with impaired RanGTP binding is defective in Crm1 loading.

claim: Structural analyses of the RanGTP:Crm1 complex bound to prototypic NESs suggest that any peptide can function as a NES as long as its backbone conformation permits its side chains to access the rigid hydrophobic pockets of Crm1.
